summary: Describes the characteristics of mobile ad hoc networks, which form without fixed infrastructure and whose nodes move, and how they differ from wired networks. It discusses what those differences mean for designing and evaluating routing protocols, with an emphasis on performance evaluation. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine a bunch of kids with walkie-talkies passing messages along while they run around. Keeping messages on course is hard when everyone moves, so this document explains the problems and how to test solutions.

questions: mobile ad hoc network routing evaluation
how do you evaluate mobile ad hoc routing protocols
subtitle: What makes mobile ad hoc networks different from wired ones, and how to judge routing protocols built for them.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols for the fixed Internet assume stable links and plentiful bandwidth, but mobile wireless nodes move, run on batteries and share weak links.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the traits of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs), the qualities a MANET routing protocol should have, and protocol-independent metrics and network contexts for evaluating them.
tldr.outcome: It sets out a common way to compare routing protocols for the IETF manet working group; it is Informational and specifies no protocol.

facts.label: Large network scale
facts.value: Tens or hundreds of nodes per routing area

today: RFC 2501 is an Informational document, and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It specifies no routing protocol and does not set an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: What a MANET Is For
sections.content:
A mobile ad hoc network (MANET) has no fixed infrastructure. Its nodes, which may be combined routers and hosts, themselves form the network routing infrastructure. This differs from mobile IP, which supports a roaming host while hop-by-hop routing still relies on routing protocols in the fixed network.

The RFC lists possible uses: industrial and commercial cooperative data exchange, mesh networks as an alternative or addition to cell-based infrastructures, military networks, wearable computing, and fire, safety and rescue operations that need rapidly deployable communications. It notes that the field is also called Mobile Packet Radio Networking, Mobile Mesh Networking or Mobile, Multihop, Wireless Networking.
sections.eli5: A MANET is a network where nobody owns the wires. The devices themselves pass messages along, like kids in a game of telephone who keep moving around.

sections.title: Characteristics of MANETs
sections.content:
MANET nodes can move arbitrarily and may sit on airplanes, ships, trucks, cars or even people. The network may run alone or attach to a fixed network, usually as a stub network that carries its own traffic but does not let outside traffic transit through. The RFC names four salient characteristics:

  • Dynamic topologies: links change randomly and rapidly, and can be unidirectional as well as bidirectional.
  • Bandwidth-constrained, variable capacity links: wireless links have much lower capacity than wired ones, so congestion is the norm rather than the exception.
  • Energy-constrained operation: nodes may run on batteries, so saving energy can be the most important design goal.
  • Limited physical security: more eavesdropping, spoofing and denial-of-service risk, though decentralized control avoids single points of failure.

Some networks may be large, with tens or hundreds of nodes per routing area, and the mechanisms for scalability in a MANET are likely different from those used elsewhere.
sections.eli5: Everyone is moving, the walkie-talkies have weak batteries and small voices, and anyone can listen in. Those four things make the game harder.

sections.title: Routing at the IP Layer
sections.content:
The IETF manet working group aims to standardize one or more intra-domain unicast routing protocols that work over a wide range of mobile networking contexts, support traditional connectionless IP service, and react efficiently to topology changes and traffic demands.

Routing at the IP layer helps when a node has several wireless interfaces, each using a different technology. The union of the separate physical topologies forms the IP routing fabric, a multigraph, and a separate node identifier ties a node's interfaces together as one mobile platform. New technologies can be added and old ones dropped without changing the routing.

For now MANETs are expected to be stub networks, which greatly reduces the route advertisement needed to work with the fixed Internet. Interoperability might combine MANET-based anycast and mobile IP.
sections.eli5: If one kid has two kinds of walkie-talkie, they can pass notes between both groups. Giving each kid one name, no matter which radio they use, keeps the notes from getting confused.

sections.title: Desirable Routing Properties
sections.content:
The RFC asks for metrics that are independent of any one protocol, starting with qualitative properties a MANET routing protocol should have:

  • Distributed operation, which it calls essential.
  • Loop-freedom, generally desirable to avoid packets circling for arbitrary time; TTL values can bound the problem but a structured approach is usually better.
  • Demand-based operation, which adapts routes to traffic and saves energy and bandwidth, at the cost of route discovery delay.
  • Proactive operation, the flip side, for contexts where that delay is unacceptable.
  • Security, since without network-level or link-layer security a protocol is open to snooping, replay, header manipulation and redirection of routing messages.
  • Sleep period operation, so nodes that stop transmitting or receiving to save energy do not break routing.
  • Unidirectional link support, valuable when two one-way links are the only connection between two regions.
sections.eli5: A good message-passing game works without a boss, avoids notes going around in circles, lets sleepy kids nap, and still works if a walkie-talkie only talks one way.

sections.title: Measuring Protocol Performance
sections.content:
The quantitative metrics are: end-to-end data throughput and delay, route acquisition time (important for on-demand protocols), the percentage of out-of-order delivery (which matters to TCP), and efficiency, the internal measure of how much overhead a protocol spends. Efficiency is tracked with ratios: data bits transmitted per data bit delivered, control bits per data bit delivered, and control and data packets per data packet delivered. Anything that is not data counts as control overhead, including data packet headers.

Results depend on the networking context, so the RFC lists parameters that should be varied: network size, connectivity (average number of neighbors), topological rate of change, link capacity, fraction of unidirectional links, traffic patterns, mobility model, and the fraction and frequency of sleeping nodes.

A protocol description should state both its advantages and limitations, since a routing protocol tends to suit some contexts better than others.
sections.eli5: To see which way of passing notes is best, count how fast and how many arrive, how many whispers were wasted, and try it with few kids, many kids, fast kids and sleepy kids.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mobile wireless networks are generally more prone to physical security threats than fixed, hardwired networks, and link-level techniques such as encryption are often used to reduce the threats. Without link-level encryption, the most pressing issue at the network layer is inter-router authentication before routing control information is exchanged.

The working group planned to explore several levels, from no security (always an option) and simple shared-key approaches up to full public key infrastructure-based authentication, and might standardize several optional authentication modes for MANETs.
sections.eli5: Because anyone can overhear walkie-talkies, the kids should check who is talking before trusting directions from them.

items.title: Dynamic topologies
items.text: Nodes move arbitrarily, so links change randomly and rapidly.

items.title: Constrained links
items.text: Lower capacity than wired links, so congestion is the norm.

items.title: Limited energy
items.text: Battery-powered nodes may need energy conservation above all.

items.title: Limited security
items.text: More exposure to eavesdropping, spoofing and denial of service.
